title: LinkedIn's Top Colleges, Workers' GDP Share Hits Record Low, and KPMG Interns Eye the C-Suite
author: Great Leadership
summary: This week's Future Ready Leadership Briefing curates three stories that the author argues together redefine what career success looks like in 2026: a LinkedIn ranking of colleges by career outcomes rather than prestige, a Reuters report that workers' share of GDP has hit its lowest level since 1947 even as productivity rises, and reporting on ambitious but anxious KPMG interns whose parents are increasingly intervening in their job searches. The curator's framing throughout is that leaders are getting the surface story (rankings, productivity gains, intern ambition) without grappling with the harder implication underneath each one — that credentials are being judged by outcomes, that productivity gains aren't reaching workers, and that early-career pressure is reshaping how young employees show up at work. This is a Pass A curated digest: each item comes with the author's own analysis rather than a bare link, so it has independent value as commentary beyond the three source articles it points to. The newsletter is aimed at HR and people leaders navigating AI, workforce readiness, and organizational culture.
points: The LinkedIn Top 50 Colleges list signals a shift from prestige-based to outcomes-based evaluation of higher education, which the author says employers should treat as a data point, not a hiring shortcut.

Workers' share of GDP hit 52.9% in Q2 2026, the lowest since records began in 1947, even as productivity grew faster than expected — the author frames this gap as a looming 'trust problem' for leaders touting AI-driven efficiency gains.
93% of KPMG's surveyed interns say they aspire to the C-suite, undercutting the common leadership assumption that young workers only want flexibility and work-life balance.

76% of those same interns believe long-term career success will require both strong human skills and the ability to direct AI agents — a specific, actionable data point for how leaders should reframe entry-level skill development.
quotes: LinkedIn ranked the 50 U.S. colleges that best set graduates up for long-term career success, with Princeton leading the list for the second year in a row.
Families are no longer just asking, "What is the most prestigious school?" They are asking, "What does this school actually help you do after graduation?
According to Bureau of Labor Statistics data cited by Reuters, labor's share of nominal GDP fell to 52.9% in the second quarter, down from 53.7% in the first quarter.
If productivity rises and employees do not feel any meaningful improvement in pay, opportunity, workload, flexibility, or career growth, the productivity story becomes a trust problem.
Nearly all respondents, 93%, said they aspire to reach the C-suite or senior executive roles during their careers.
76% said long-term success will require both strong human skills and the ability to direct AI agents effectively.
Parents calling employers crosses a line, but it also says something about the pressure young workers are under.
